lead.headline: Riyadh Airport Partly Reopens as Houthi Missiles Keep Coming
lead.deck: Saudi forces intercept a missile and a drone aimed at the capital on the day two terminals restart.
body: Saudi Arabia reopened two terminals at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Sunday 25 October. Terminal 1 handles domestic flights and Terminal 2 international ones. The airport had been shut for about two weeks after strikes earlier in October by the Houthis, an armed group from Yemen, Saudi Arabia's southern neighbour, which is backed by Iran.

The attacks did not stop for the reopening. On the same day the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a ballistic missile launched towards Riyadh and destroyed a drone aimed at the capital. It also reported intercepting ten ballistic missiles aimed at the kingdom's southern region. A Houthi spokesman called the airport unsafe and said it remained a “military target”.

Airlines are moving cautiously. Emirates says its flights to Riyadh and Dammam are due to resume on 8 November. The United States has ordered its non-emergency government staff out of Saudi Arabia as the attacks worsened, and American embassies across the region have tightened security over warnings of Iranian plots. The US administration has said it will hold off on renewed strikes on Iran until after its 3 November midterm elections.

Markets are pricing the risk. Brent crude closed at $116.72 a barrel on Friday 23 October, its highest close since 29 April, and India's Sensex fell for a fourth straight session. The Economy page explains the numbers.

lead.why: Saudi Arabia is one of the world's largest oil exporters. Attacks on its capital add to the risk built into the price of every barrel India imports, and disrupt flights between India and the Gulf, where many Indians live and work.

world.headline: Kim Jong Un Crosses a New Bridge Into China as Trade Ties Warm
world.deck: The 3 km New Yalu River Bridge opened this month after years of delay.
body: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday 24 October, crossing the newly opened New Yalu River Bridge. The Yalu River marks part of the border between the two countries, and Dandong sits on its Chinese bank.

China sent a senior figure to meet him. Wang Huning, China's fourth-highest-ranked official, accompanied Kim and conveyed greetings from President Xi Jinping. Kim toured a Dandong automobile factory and paid tribute to Chinese soldiers at a Korean War memorial, a reminder that Chinese troops fought on North Korea's side in that war.

The bridge is about trade, and it has been a long time coming. Construction finished in 2014, but it stayed closed because connecting roads and border facilities on the North Korean side were unfinished. China and North Korea finally marked its opening, at their most significant land border crossing, with a joint ceremony on 15 October.

The 3 km crossing is expected to carry heavy equipment, raw materials and energy products, with two-way traffic around the clock. China already accounts for about 95% of North Korea's total official trade.

That worries some observers. North Korea is the world's most-sanctioned country, and some fear the bridge will help it evade bans on exporting its raw materials and other goods. Other analysts say the bridge is unlikely to bring an immediate return to the level of trade before sanctions.

Sanctions, bans on trade imposed to punish a country, are why every new road into North Korea is watched closely.

india.headline: Cyclone Arnab Set to Cross the Andhra Pradesh Coast on 28 October
india.deck: A red alert in southern Odisha, schools shut in five districts and rescue teams on standby.
body: A depression, an area of low air pressure, over the Bay of Bengal is expected to strengthen into Cyclone Arnab. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) expects it to cross the coast between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh by the forenoon of 28 October as a very severe cyclonic storm.

At landfall, the point where the storm's centre crosses onto land, maximum sustained winds are forecast at 115 to 125 km an hour, gusting to 140. Heavy to very heavy rain is forecast over coastal Andhra Pradesh from 27 to 29 October.

Odisha, to the north, is preparing even without a direct hit. The IMD has issued a red alert there, and schools, colleges and Anganwadi centres in Ganjam, Gajapati, Rayagada, Koraput and Malkangiri districts will close on 28 and 29 October. Around 60 Odisha Disaster Rapid Action Force teams, 17 National Disaster Response Force teams and 225 Fire Services teams are on alert.
In Andhra Pradesh, Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu directed officials to be on high alert, and the state has kept 25,000 electric poles and other materials ready to restore power.

illustration.subtitle: Landfall due 28 October

india.why: India's east coast faces cyclones almost every year. Forecasts days ahead, school closures and pre-positioned rescue teams are the tools of disaster management that turn a dangerous storm into a manageable one.

politics_and_civics.headline: Serbia's Snap Election Pits Students Against Aleksandar Vucic
politics_and_civics.deck: Almost two years of protests become a contest for all 250 seats in parliament.
body: In 2024 a canopy at a newly renovated railway station in Novi Sad collapsed and killed 16 people. Students led protests that lasted almost two years, against alleged corruption and authoritarianism. On Sunday 25 October those protests turned into a snap election, one called before it was due, for Serbia's 250-seat parliament.

Serbia's system is proportional. All 250 seats are elected in a single nationwide constituency, and a list generally needs at least 3% of the vote to enter parliament. The student list fielded 250 candidates, many of them academics or political outsiders, led by cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic and running on an anti-corruption platform.

Their opponent is the SNS party of Aleksandar Vucic, Serbia's longtime leader, who resigned as president in September to run for prime minister. Reuters called the vote the biggest challenge to his rule for more than a decade. An Ipsos poll gave the SNS 47% and the students 40%, but other polls put the students ahead, and Serbia lacks reliable independent polling.

Both sides raised concerns. Opponents of Vucic and some independent monitoring groups warned of possible irregularities in the voting, while Vucic warned that protests claiming fraud would be quashed. Polls closed at 8pm local time, and the official tally is not expected before Monday.

Democracy was at work in the United States too. More than 18 million Americans had voted early, by mail or in person, by 22 October, according to the University of Florida's Election Lab count cited by ABC News, ahead of the 3 November midterms. NBC News's tracker later counted 27,878,423 early votes. ABC News found Democrats make up a much larger share of early ballots so far, but cautioned that early votes are only one piece of the puzzle.

illustration.subtitle: 250 seats, 3% threshold
illustration.caption: The official tally is not expected before Monday.

politics_and_civics.why: It tests whether a street movement can turn into a parliamentary force, and how electoral rules such as a single national constituency and a 3% threshold shape who wins seats.

economics.headline: Brent Closes at $116.72, Its Highest Since April
economics.deck: A third straight weekly gain as traders price in Gulf attacks and possible US strikes on Iran.
body: Brent crude, the benchmark for oil traded worldwide, gained 3.1% on Friday 23 October to settle at $116.72 a barrel, its highest close since 29 April. US crude, West Texas Intermediate (WTI), rose 3.8% to $103.27. Brent rose 6.2% over the week, its third straight weekly gain.

Three worries drove it. The Houthis kept attacking Saudi Arabia, a reported oil spill off the United Arab Emirates added to supply concerns, and traders priced in renewed US strikes on Iran. US officials told The New York Times that the US and Israel have plans for fresh strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections.

India felt it the same day. The Sensex fell 125.56 points, or 0.17%, to 73,123.83, its fourth straight losing session, and the Nifty fell 87.65 points, or 0.39%, as crude passed $114 amid tension in West Asia. India imports most of its crude, so higher oil prices feed into fuel costs, inflation and the import bill.

Gold moved the other way. Spot gold fell about 4% over the week to below $4,000 an ounce, at $3,993.96, and in India 24-carat gold cost Rs 14,258 a gram on 24 October, its first rise in five days. Analysts linked gold's weakness to the oil rally: dearer crude revives inflation worries and strengthens expectations that interest rates will stay higher for longer, which makes gold, an asset that pays no interest, less attractive.

science_and_technology.headline: Dwarf Reedsnakes Roll Like Wheels, Four Times Faster Than They Slither
science_and_technology.deck: High-speed video shows how tiny snakes escape by cartwheeling.
body: Escaping a predator is a matter of speed. Most snakes move by lateral undulation, the familiar side-to-side slither. Dwarf reedsnakes, small snakes from Southeast Asia, have another option: they roll like a wheel. A study in the journal Current Biology by Yosuke Kojima and colleagues at Toho University in Japan has now filmed them from several angles to measure how.

The behaviour itself was not new to science. In 2023, a Malaysian and US team described the dwarf reed snake Pseudorabdion longiceps actively cartwheeling, launching coils of its body into the air and rolling down slopes. The new study, which features the species Pseudorabdion saravacense, goes further by measuring the movement in detail.

Rolling is fast. The snakes reached peak speeds of 1.72 to 3.69 metres per second while rolling, about four times their peak speed when slithering, and could stay on a test track only 20 centimetres wide.

The secret is coordination. Each cycle, a snake swings an arched section of its body down past its head, a move the researchers call a “stroke”, while its head stays pointed in the direction of travel at a fairly constant height. The researchers suggest that keeping the head steady may help the snakes stay in control at high speed.

explainer.title: How India names and warns about cyclones
body: Cyclones in the north Indian Ocean are named from a list agreed by the countries of the region, so that warnings are easy to follow and remember. The India Meteorological Department, which serves as the regional centre for cyclone forecasts, tracks a weather system as it grows from a low-pressure area into a depression and then into a cyclonic storm, and gives the storm its name at that stage.

Warnings are colour-coded. Green means no action, yellow means be aware, orange means be prepared, and red means take action. A red alert, like the one for southern Odisha this week, tells district officials to act: closing schools, moving people to shelters and placing rescue teams where they will be needed.

lead.headline: Riyadh's Airport Opens Again as Attacks Go On
body: Riyadh is the capital of Saudi Arabia. Its main airport had been shut for about two weeks after attacks. On Sunday, two of its terminals opened again.
The attacks come from the Houthis, an armed group in Yemen. On the same day, Saudi forces said they stopped a missile and a drone aimed at Riyadh.
Some airlines are waiting. Emirates plans to fly to Riyadh again on 8 November. The trouble has also pushed up the price of oil.

world.headline: Kim Jong Un Crosses a New Bridge to China
body: Kim Jong Un leads North Korea. On Saturday he crossed a new bridge into China and visited the city of Dandong.
The bridge is 3 km long. It crosses the Yalu River, which marks part of the border. It is meant to carry far more trade.
China is North Korea's biggest trading partner, with about 95% of its official trade. Some people worry the bridge will help North Korea break trade bans.

india.headline: A Big Storm Heads for Andhra Pradesh
body: A cyclone is a giant spinning storm. One called Arnab is expected to reach the coast of Andhra Pradesh on 28 October.
Its winds could gust up to 140 km an hour. Lots of rain is expected too.
Odisha will close schools in five districts. Rescue teams are ready, and Andhra Pradesh has 25,000 electric poles ready to fix power lines.

politics_and_civics.headline: Serbia Votes in a Big Election
body: Serbia is a country in Europe. In 2024 a roof at a train station fell down, and 16 people died.
Students protested for almost two years against leaders they said were dishonest. On Sunday, Serbia held an early election for all 250 seats in its parliament.
The students backed their own list. They faced the party of Aleksandar Vucic, Serbia's longtime leader. Polls did not agree on who was ahead.

economics.headline: Oil Costs the Most Since April
body: Oil prices are counted per barrel. On Friday the world price, called Brent, closed at $116.72. That is the highest since 29 April.
People worried about attacks on Saudi Arabia and about new US strikes on Iran. Worried buyers pushed the price up.
India buys most of its oil from abroad. On the same day, a main measure of Indian share prices fell for the fourth day in a row.

science_and_technology.headline: Tiny Snakes That Roll Like Wheels
body: Most snakes slither from side to side. Dwarf reedsnakes from Southeast Asia can also roll, like a wheel, to escape danger.
Scientists in Japan filmed them. Rolling, the snakes went about four times faster than when they slithered.
Their heads stayed steady, facing forward, while the rest of the body swung round and round. That may help them stay in control at speed.
